statement: Let $A \subseteq B \subseteq C$ be commutative rings with $A$ [Noetherian](c:noetherian-ring). If $C$ is a [finitely generated algebra](c:finitely-generated-algebra) over $A$ and a [finitely generated module](c:finitely-generated-module) over $B$, then $B$ is a finitely generated algebra over $A$.

hypotheses.text: The rings satisfy $A \subseteq B \subseteq C$, all commutative, so $B \to C$ is injective.
The ring $A$ is [Noetherian](c:noetherian-ring).
The ring $C$ is a [finitely generated algebra](c:finitely-generated-algebra) over $A$.
The ring $C$ is a [finitely generated module](c:finitely-generated-module) over $B$.

formal.difference: Mathlib states it for algebras $A \to B \to C$ with a scalar tower and an injective map $B \to C$. Subrings give the case of inclusions.

proofs.name: Finite coefficient subring
proofs.slogan: Collect the finitely many coefficients that express $C$ over $B$, adjoin them to $A$, and use Noetherianity to make $B$ finite over that subring.
proofs.scope: The whole lemma. Both module generators and algebra generators are finite lists, so the coefficient list is finite.

roles.why: Injectivity lets $B$ be read as a submodule of $C$ over the subring $B_0$.
Noetherianity of $A$ passes to the finitely generated subalgebra $B_0$.
The algebra generators $x_i$ of $C$ are the elements rewritten through module generators.
The module generators $y_j$ supply the coefficients $b_{ij}$ and $b_{ijk}$.

steps.slogan: Write the algebra generators and the products of module generators through the module generators.
steps.detail: Let $x_1, \dots, x_m$ generate $C$ as an $A$-algebra and let $y_1 = 1, y_2, \dots, y_n$ generate $C$ as a $B$-module. Choose $b_{ij}, b_{ijk} \in B$ with $x_i = \sum_j b_{ij} y_j$ and $y_i y_j = \sum_k b_{ijk} y_k$.

steps.slogan: Adjoin all coefficients $b_{ij}$ and $b_{ijk}$ to $A$ to form a Noetherian subalgebra $B_0 \subseteq B$.
steps.detail: The subalgebra $B_0 = A[b_{ij}, b_{ijk}]$ of $B$ is a quotient of a [polynomial ring](c:polynomial-ring) in finitely many variables over $A$. This ring is Noetherian by the Hilbert basis theorem, so $B_0$ is Noetherian.

steps.slogan: Show that $y_1, \dots, y_n$ generate $C$ as a module over $B_0$.
steps.detail: Let $M = \sum_j B_0 y_j$. It contains $1 = y_1$ and every product $y_i y_j$, so $M$ is a subring of $C$. It contains each $x_i$, so it contains the $A$-algebra generated by them. Hence $M = C$.

steps.slogan: View $B$ as a submodule of the [Noetherian module](c:noetherian-module) $C$ over $B_0$.
steps.detail: By step 3, $C$ is a finitely generated module over the Noetherian ring $B_0$, so it is a Noetherian module. The injective $B_0$-linear map $B \to C$ makes $B$ a submodule of $C$, so $B$ is a Noetherian module and a finitely generated $B_0$-module.

steps.slogan: Combine the generators of $B$ over $B_0$ with those of $B_0$ over $A$.
steps.detail: If $B = \sum_k B_0 z_k$ and $B_0 = A[b_1, \dots, b_r]$, then every element of $B$ is a polynomial over $A$ in $b_1, \dots, b_r, z_1, \dots, z_s$. So $B$ is a finitely generated $A$-algebra.

concepts.c:noetherian-ring: Noetherian rings give finite generation of submodules and survive finitely generated extension.
concepts.c:finitely-generated-algebra: Finite algebra generators give the finite list of coefficients.
concepts.c:finitely-generated-module: Finite module generators over $B$ define the coefficients $b_{ij}$.
concepts.c:polynomial-ring: A quotient of a polynomial ring over $A$ is Noetherian.
concepts.c:noetherian-module: Submodules of Noetherian modules are finitely generated.

statement: Let $f$ be a smooth self-map of a [compact manifold](c:compact-manifold) $X$ whose [fixed points](c:fixed-point) $p$ are nondegenerate. Let $T$ be an endomorphism of an [elliptic complex](c:elliptic-complex) $E$ over $X$ that covers $f$, with fibre maps $\varphi_{i,p}$ at fixed points. Then its [Lefschetz number](c:lefschetz-number) is $\sum_{f(p)=p} \sum_i (-1)^i \operatorname{tr}\varphi_{i,p} \,/\, |\det(1 - df_p)|$.

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is a [compact manifold](c:compact-manifold).
The map $f \colon X \to X$ is smooth and each [fixed point](c:fixed-point) $p$ is nondegenerate: $\det(1 - df_p) \neq 0$.
The complex $E$ is [elliptic](c:elliptic-complex), and $T$ is a chain endomorphism of $E$ covering $f$, built from bundle maps $\varphi_i \colon f^*E^i \to E^i$.

proofs.name: Supertrace localization at fixed points
proofs.slogan: Write the Lefschetz number as a supertrace of smoothing operators and let their kernels concentrate at the fixed points.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof; the symbol calculus in steps 3 and 4 rests on the cited work. The applications of part II are not needed here.

roles.why: Compactness makes cohomology finite dimensional, kernels trace class, and fixed points finite in number.
Nondegenerate fixed points are isolated and give the local factor $1/|\det(1 - df_p)|$.
Ellipticity gives a parametrix and finite cohomology, and the chain map $T$ acts on cohomology.

steps.slogan: Express the [Lefschetz number](c:lefschetz-number) as a supertrace of $T$ composed with a smoothing operator.
steps.detail: By ellipticity a parametrix of $E$ gives smoothing operators $S$ on the complex that are chain homotopic to the identity. The Hopf trace argument then gives $L(T) = \sum_i (-1)^i \operatorname{tr}(T_i S_i)$ for every such $S$.

steps.slogan: Compute the supertrace as an integral of the kernel along the diagonal.
steps.detail: The operator $T_i S_i$ has a smooth kernel, and its trace is the integral of the fibre trace of this kernel over the diagonal. Because $T$ composes with $f$, the integrand evaluates the kernel of $S$ at the pair $(f(x), x)$.

steps.slogan: Choose smoothing operators whose kernels approach the identity, so the integral concentrates where $f(x) = x$.
steps.detail: Take smoothing operators $S_t$ whose kernels converge to the kernel of the identity, and let $t \to 0$. The graph of $f$ meets the diagonal only at fixed points, so the integral outside any neighbourhood of the fixed points tends to $0$. By step 1 the supertrace does not depend on $t$.

steps.slogan: Evaluate the limit at one nondegenerate fixed point by a local computation.
steps.detail: In coordinates near $p$, write $f(x) \approx p + df_p(x - p)$. The change of variables $u = x - f(x)$ has Jacobian $\det(1 - df_p)$, so the local integral of the kernel gives $\sum_i (-1)^i \operatorname{tr}\varphi_{i,p} / |\det(1 - df_p)|$.

steps.slogan: Add the local contributions of the finitely many fixed points.
steps.detail: Nondegenerate fixed points are isolated, so there are finitely many in the [compact manifold](c:compact-manifold). The sum of their contributions is the limit of step 3, and so equals $L(T)$.

concepts.c:compact-manifold: Compactness gives trace-class kernels and finitely many isolated fixed points.
concepts.c:fixed-point: The formula localizes the trace at the fixed points of $f$.
concepts.c:elliptic-complex: Ellipticity gives a parametrix and finite-dimensional cohomology.
concepts.c:lefschetz-number: The Lefschetz number is the alternating trace that the formula computes.

source.ref: M. F. Atiyah and R. Bott, A Lefschetz fixed point formula for elliptic complexes: I, Annals of Mathematics 86 (1967), 374-407
source.note: Part I proves the formula for elliptic complexes through the supertrace of smoothing operators; part II (Annals of Mathematics 88 (1968), 451-491) gives the applications.

statement: Let $X$ be a sample with a family of distributions $P_\theta$. If a statistic $T$ is a boundedly [complete](c:complete-statistic) [sufficient statistic](c:sufficient-statistic) for $\theta$ and a statistic $S$ is [ancillary](c:ancillary-statistic), then $T$ and $S$ are [independent](c:independent-random-variables) under every $P_\theta$.

hypotheses.text: The statistic $T$ is [sufficient](c:sufficient-statistic): the conditional law of $X$ given $T$ is the same for every $\theta$.
The statistic $T$ is boundedly [complete](c:complete-statistic): if $h$ is bounded and $E_\theta h(T) = 0$ for all $\theta$, then $h(T) = 0$ almost surely under every $P_\theta$.
The statistic $S$ is [ancillary](c:ancillary-statistic): the law of $S$ is the same for every $\theta$.

conclusion: For every $\theta$, the statistics $T$ and $S$ are [independent](c:independent-random-variables) under $P_\theta$.

proofs.name: Constant conditional probability
proofs.slogan: Show with bounded completeness that the conditional probability of an event of $S$ given $T$ is constant, then factor the joint probability.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The events of $S$ and of $T$ are arbitrary measurable sets, so independence follows from the product formula.

roles.why: Ancillarity makes $p = P_\theta(S \in A)$ the same for every $\theta$.
Sufficiency lets the conditional probability be chosen as a function $g(T)$ free of $\theta$.
Bounded completeness turns zero mean of $g(T) - p$ into $g(T) = p$ almost surely.

steps.slogan: Fix a measurable event $A$ of $S$ and let $p = P_\theta(S \in A)$.
steps.detail: By ancillarity the number $p$ is the same for every $\theta$. It is the constant that the conditional probability must equal.

steps.slogan: Take the [conditional probability](c:conditional-probability) of $\{S \in A\}$ given $T$ and see that it is free of $\theta$.
steps.detail: The statistic $S$ is a function of $X$, and the conditional law of $X$ given $T$ is the same for every $\theta$. So there is one measurable function $g$ with $0 \le g \le 1$ and $g(T) = P_\theta(S \in A \mid T)$ for every $\theta$.

steps.slogan: Show that the bounded function $g(T) - p$ has expectation zero for every $\theta$.
steps.detail: The tower property gives $E_\theta[g(T)] = P_\theta(S \in A) = p$ for all $\theta$. So $h = g - p$ is bounded and satisfies $E_\theta h(T) = 0$ for all $\theta$.

steps.slogan: Conclude from bounded completeness that $g(T) = p$ almost surely.
steps.detail: The function $h = g - p$ of step 3 is bounded with zero mean for all $\theta$. Bounded completeness of $T$ gives $h(T) = 0$ almost surely under each $P_\theta$.

steps.slogan: Factor the joint probability of $\{S \in A\}$ and $\{T \in B\}$ for every measurable $B$.
steps.detail: By step 4, $P_\theta(S \in A, T \in B) = E_\theta[1_B(T) g(T)] = p \, P_\theta(T \in B) = P_\theta(S \in A) P_\theta(T \in B)$. The events $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary, so $T$ and $S$ are independent.

concepts.c:complete-statistic: Bounded completeness forces the zero-mean function $g(T) - p$ to vanish.
concepts.c:sufficient-statistic: Sufficiency removes $\theta$ from the conditional probability.
concepts.c:ancillary-statistic: Ancillarity makes the probability $p$ free of $\theta$.
concepts.c:independent-random-variables: The product formula for all events is independence of $T$ and $S$.
concepts.c:conditional-probability: The conditional probability given $T$ is the function $g(T)$.

source.note: The standard proof of Basu (1955), as in Casella and Berger, Statistical Inference, section 6.2.

statement: Let $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ be a [simply connected](c:simply-connected-space) open region, $f$ a $C^1$ [planar vector field](c:planar-vector-field) on $D$ and $\varphi \colon D \to \mathbb{R}$ a $C^1$ function. If the [divergence](c:divergence) of $\varphi f$ has one sign and vanishes identically on no open set, then $\dot{x} = f(x)$ has no nonconstant [periodic orbit](c:periodic-orbit) in $D$.

hypotheses.text: The region $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ is open and [simply connected](c:simply-connected-space).
The [planar vector field](c:planar-vector-field) $f$ and the function $\varphi$ are $C^1$ on $D$.
The [divergence](c:divergence) $\nabla \cdot (\varphi f)$ is nonnegative on $D$, or nonpositive on $D$, and vanishes identically on no open subset.

conclusion: No nonconstant [periodic orbit](c:periodic-orbit) of $\dot{x} = f(x)$ lies entirely in $D$.

proofs.name: Green's theorem on the enclosed region
proofs.slogan: A periodic orbit would carry zero flux of $\varphi f$, while Green's theorem gives the integral of a nonzero one-signed divergence.
proofs.scope: The whole criterion. A constant orbit is an equilibrium and is excluded by the statement.

roles.why: Simple connectivity puts the region enclosed by the orbit inside $D$.
The $C^1$ field has unique solutions, so the orbit is a simple closed curve, and Green's theorem applies.
A one-signed divergence that vanishes on no open set has a nonzero integral over the enclosed region.

steps.slogan: Suppose a periodic orbit $\gamma$ lies in $D$ and take the region $R$ that it encloses.
steps.detail: By uniqueness of solutions, a nonconstant periodic orbit does not cross itself, so $\gamma$ is a [Jordan curve](c:jordan-curve). It bounds a region $R$, and $R \subseteq D$ because $D$ is simply connected.

steps.slogan: Show that the field $\varphi f$ has zero flux through $\gamma$.
steps.detail: Parametrize $\gamma$ by a solution $(x(t), y(t))$ with period $\tau$. The flux is $\oint \varphi (f_1\,dy - f_2\,dx) = \int_0^\tau \varphi (f_1 f_2 - f_2 f_1)\,dt = 0$, because $(\dot x, \dot y) = (f_1, f_2)$.

steps.slogan: Turn the zero flux into a zero integral of the divergence over $R$.
steps.detail: Green's theorem in divergence form gives $\iint_R \nabla \cdot (\varphi f)\,dA = \oint_\gamma \varphi (f_1\,dy - f_2\,dx)$. By step 2 the right side is $0$.

steps.slogan: Show that a one-signed continuous divergence with zero integral vanishes on the open set $R$.
steps.detail: The function $\nabla \cdot (\varphi f)$ is continuous and, say, nonnegative. If it were positive at one point of $R$, it would be positive on a small disc, and its integral would be positive. So it vanishes on the open set $R$, against the hypothesis.

concepts.c:simply-connected-space: It puts the interior of the orbit inside $D$.
concepts.c:planar-vector-field: The orbit is a solution curve tangent to the field.
concepts.c:divergence: The divergence of $\varphi f$ is the integrand of Green's theorem.
concepts.c:periodic-orbit: Its existence leads to a contradiction.
concepts.c:jordan-curve: A simple closed orbit encloses a region by the Jordan curve theorem.

source.note: The standard Green's theorem proof of Dulac's criterion, as in Strogatz, Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos, section 7.2.

statement: A topological space $X$ is [metrizable](c:metrizable-space) if and only if it is [regular](c:regular-space) and [Hausdorff](c:hausdorff-space) and has a base that is a countable union of [locally finite families](c:locally-finite-family).

hypotheses.text: $X$ is a topological space.

conclusion: $X$ is metrizable exactly when it is regular, Hausdorff and has a $\sigma$-locally finite base.

proofs.name: Embedding into a sup-metric space
proofs.slogan: Metric spaces are regular with locally finite bases; conversely, a locally finite base gives functions that embed the space in a sup-metric space.
proofs.scope: The Nagata-Smirnov form that the sources state; Bing's form with discrete families is not proved here. Step 1 proves necessity and steps 2 to 6 prove sufficiency.

roles.why: Every step works with open sets, closures and bases of the topology of $X$.

steps.slogan: Show that a metric space is regular and Hausdorff with a $\sigma$-locally finite base.
steps.detail: Balls separate points, and $\overline{B}(x, r) \subseteq B(x, 2r)$ gives regularity. A metric space is [paracompact](c:paracompact-space) (A. H. Stone), so the cover by balls of radius $1/m$ has a locally finite open refinement $\mathcal{A}_m$. If $B(x, 3/m) \subseteq U$ and $x \in A \in \mathcal{A}_m$, then $A \subseteq U$, so $\bigcup_m \mathcal{A}_m$ is a base.

steps.slogan: Write each open set $W$ as a union of open sets whose closures lie in $W$.
steps.detail: Let $\mathcal{B} = \bigcup_n \mathcal{B}_n$ be the base. Put $G_n = \bigcup \{B \in \mathcal{B}_n : \overline{B} \subseteq W\}$. Local finiteness gives $\overline{G_n} = \bigcup \overline{B} \subseteq W$, and regularity gives $W = \bigcup_n G_n$, so $W$ is also a countable union of closed sets.

steps.slogan: Show that the space is [normal](c:normal-space) by separating closed sets with shrunken unions.
steps.detail: For disjoint closed $A, D$ write $X \setminus D = \bigcup G_n$ and $X \setminus A = \bigcup H_n$ as in step 2. Then $G'_n = G_n \setminus \bigcup_{i \le n} \overline{H_i}$ and $H'_n = H_n \setminus \bigcup_{i \le n} \overline{G_i}$ are open, and $\bigcup G'_n \supseteq A$ and $\bigcup H'_n \supseteq D$ are disjoint.

steps.slogan: Build a continuous function $f_B \colon X \to [0, 1/n]$ that is positive exactly on $B \in \mathcal{B}_n$.
steps.detail: Write $B = \bigcup_k F_k$ with closed $F_k$ by step 2. Urysohn's lemma in the normal space gives continuous $g_k \colon X \to [0,1]$ equal to $1$ on $F_k$ and $0$ off $B$. Then $f_B = \frac{1}{n}\sum_k 2^{-k} g_k$ is continuous and positive exactly on $B$.

steps.slogan: Show that the map $F(x) = (f_B(x))_B$ is continuous for the sup metric.
steps.detail: Index the coordinates by pairs $(n, B)$ with $B \in \mathcal{B}_n$, and use $\rho(z, w) = \sup |z_B - w_B|$. Fix $x_0$ and $\varepsilon > 0$, and take $N$ with $1/N < \varepsilon/2$. For $n > N$ every $f_B$ with $B \in \mathcal{B}_n$ stays within $1/n < \varepsilon/2$ of $f_B(x_0)$. For $n \le N$, a neighbourhood of $x_0$ meets finitely many $B \in \mathcal{B}_n$, so finitely many coordinates are not zero there, and each is continuous.

steps.slogan: Show that $F$ is injective and open onto its image, so it is an [embedding](c:embedding-of-topological-spaces).
steps.detail:
For $x 
eq y$ choose open $U$ with $x \in U

i y$ and $B \in \mathcal{B}_n$ with $x \in B \subseteq U$, so $f_B(x) > 0 = f_B(y)$. For $x \in U$ open with $x \in B \subseteq U$, the set $\{z : z_B > 0\} \cap F(X)$ is open and lies in $F(U)$.

steps.slogan: Join the two directions into the equivalence.
steps.detail: Step 1 shows that every metrizable space has the three properties. By steps 5 and 6, a regular Hausdorff space with a $\sigma$-locally finite base is homeomorphic to a subspace of a metric space, so it is metrizable.

concepts.c:metrizable-space: Metrizability is the property that both directions prove or use.
concepts.c:regular-space: Regularity gives the shrinking of open sets and the separation of points.
concepts.c:hausdorff-space: Hausdorff separation makes the functions $f_B$ separate points.
concepts.c:locally-finite-family: Local finiteness makes the closure of a union and the sup-metric continuity work.
concepts.c:paracompact-space: Stone's theorem gives the locally finite refinements of ball covers.
concepts.c:normal-space: Normality lets Urysohn's lemma build the functions $f_B$.
concepts.c:embedding-of-topological-spaces: An embedding into a metric space is what metrizes $X$.

source.note: The proof of Munkres, Topology, 2nd edition, Theorem 40.3 (the Nagata-Smirnov metrization theorem).

statement: Let $f \colon (0, \infty) \to (0, \infty)$ satisfy $f(1) = 1$ and the [functional equation](c:functional-equation) $f(x+1) = x f(x)$ for $x > 0$, and let $\log f$ be convex. Then $f(x) = \Gamma(x)$ for every $x > 0$, where $\Gamma$ is the [gamma function](c:gamma-function).

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is positive: $f(x) > 0$ for every $x > 0$.
The function $f$ satisfies $f(1) = 1$.
The function $f$ satisfies the [functional equation](c:functional-equation) $f(x+1) = x f(x)$ for every $x > 0$.
The function $f$ is [log-convex](c:log-convex-function): $\log f$ is convex on $(0, \infty)$.

proofs.name: Gauss limit sandwich
proofs.slogan: Squeeze $\log f(x)$ between chord and slope bounds of a convex function to get the Gauss limit formula, which fixes $f$ and also fixes $\Gamma$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The limit is first shown for $0 < x \le 1$ and then for all $x > 0$ by the functional equation.

roles.why: Positivity makes $\varphi = \log f$ defined on $(0, \infty)$.
The value $f(1) = 1$ gives $\varphi(1) = 0$, which fixes the limit.
The [functional equation](c:functional-equation) gives the recursion $\varphi(x+1) = \varphi(x) + \log x$.
Convexity of $\varphi$ gives the chord and slope bounds on $[n, n+1]$.

steps.slogan: Turn the functional equation into a recursion for $\varphi = \log f$.
steps.detail: Taking logarithms gives $\varphi(y+1) = \varphi(y) + \log y$ and $\varphi(1) = 0$. By induction, $\varphi(n) = \log (n-1)!$ and $\varphi(x+n) = \varphi(x) + \sum_{m=0}^{n-1} \log(x+m)$.

steps.slogan: Bound $\varphi(n+x)$ for $0 < x \le 1$ by the chord and the slope of the convex function $\varphi$.
steps.detail: The chord from $n$ to $n+1$ gives $\varphi(n+x) \le \varphi(n) + x \log n$. Slope monotonicity on $n-1 < n < n+x$ gives $\varphi(n+x) \ge \varphi(n) + x \log(n-1)$ for $n \ge 2$. Both use $\varphi(n+1) - \varphi(n) = \log n$.

steps.slogan: Squeeze $\varphi(x)$ for $0 < x \le 1$ between two sequences with the same limit.
steps.detail: Let $\ell_n(x) = x \log n + \log n! - \sum_{m=0}^{n} \log(x+m)$. Steps 1 and 2 give $\varphi(1) + \ell_n(x) \le \varphi(x) \le \varphi(1) + x \log\frac{n+1}{n} + \ell_n(x)$. Since $x \log\frac{n+1}{n} \to 0$ and $\varphi(1) = 0$, we get $\ell_n(x) \to \varphi(x)$.

steps.slogan: Extend the limit from $(0, 1]$ to all $x > 0$ by induction with the recursion.
steps.detail: A direct computation gives $\ell_n(x+1) = \ell_{n+1}(x) + \log x - (x+1)\log\frac{n+1}{n}$. So if $\ell_n(x) \to \varphi(x)$ then $\ell_n(x+1) \to \varphi(x) + \log x = \varphi(x+1)$. Hence $\ell_n(x) \to \log f(x)$ for every $x > 0$.

steps.slogan: Apply the same limit to $\Gamma$ and compare the two limits.
steps.detail: The [gamma function](c:gamma-function) is positive, $\Gamma(1) = 1$, $\Gamma(x+1) = x\Gamma(x)$, and $\log\Gamma$ is convex. So $\ell_n(x) \to \log\Gamma(x)$ as well. Limits are unique, so $\log f(x) = \log\Gamma(x)$, and positivity gives $f(x) = \Gamma(x)$.

concepts.c:functional-equation: It gives the recursion for $\log f$ at all shifts $x+n$.
concepts.c:gamma-function: $\Gamma$ satisfies all hypotheses, so it has the same limit formula.
concepts.c:log-convex-function: Convexity of $\log f$ gives the two-sided bounds on $[n, n+1]$.

statement: Let $R, M > 0$ and let $f$ be [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on the disc $|z| < R$ with $\operatorname{Re} f \le M$ there. Then for $|z| < R$, $|f(z)| \le \dfrac{2M|z|}{R - |z|} + \dfrac{|f(0)|\,(R + |z|)}{R - |z|}$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on the open disc $|z| < R$, where $R > 0$.
The [real part](c:real-part) of $f$ satisfies $\operatorname{Re} f(z) \le M$ on the disc, where $M > 0$.

proofs.name: Schwarz lemma after a half-plane map
proofs.slogan: Shift to $f(0)=0$, map the half plane $\operatorname{Re} w \le M'$ into the unit disc, apply the Schwarz lemma and invert.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for every $f(0)$. The shift in step 1 reduces it to the case $f(0) = 0$.

roles.why: [Holomorphy](c:holomorphic-function) makes $w$ holomorphic, as the Schwarz lemma needs.
The bound on the [real part](c:real-part) puts $w$ in the closed unit disc and keeps $2M' - g \ne 0$.

steps.slogan: Subtract $f(0)$ to get $g$ with $g(0) = 0$ and $\operatorname{Re} g \le M'$.
steps.detail: Put $g = f - f(0)$ and $M' = M + |f(0)|$. Then $\operatorname{Re} g = \operatorname{Re} f - \operatorname{Re} f(0) \le M + |f(0)| = M'$, and $M' > 0$.

steps.slogan: Map $g$ into the closed unit disc by $w = g/(2M' - g)$.
steps.detail: From $\operatorname{Re} g \le M'$ we get $|2M' - g|^2 - |g|^2 = 4M'(M' - \operatorname{Re} g) \ge 0$, so $|g| \le |2M' - g|$. Hence $2M' - g \ne 0$, because $M' > 0$. So $w$ is holomorphic with $|w| \le 1$ and $w(0) = 0$.

steps.slogan: Bound $|w(z)|$ by the Schwarz lemma on the disc of radius $R$.
steps.detail: The map $w$ sends the disc $|z| < R$ into the closed unit disc and fixes $0$. The Schwarz lemma, rescaled from radius $1$ to radius $R$, gives $|w(z)| \le |z|/R < 1$.

steps.slogan: Solve $w = g/(2M' - g)$ for $g$ and bound $|g(z)|$ through $|w(z)|$.
steps.detail: Solving gives $g = 2M'w/(1+w)$. Since $|w| < 1$, we get $|g| \le 2M'|w|/(1 - |w|)$, and this increases with $|w|$. With $|w| \le |z|/R$ it gives $|g(z)| \le 2M'|z|/(R - |z|)$.

steps.slogan: Add $f(0)$ back and simplify to the stated bound for $f$.
steps.detail: We have $|f| \le |g| + |f(0)| \le 2(M + |f(0)|)|z|/(R - |z|) + |f(0)|$. Putting everything over $R - |z|$ gives $\big(2M|z| + |f(0)|(R + |z|)\big)/(R - |z|)$.

concepts.c:holomorphic-function: The Schwarz lemma needs $w$ to be holomorphic on the disc.
concepts.c:real-part: The bound on the real part puts $w$ in the unit disc.

source.note: mathlib proves borelCaratheodory_zero with dist_le_div_mul_dist_of_mapsTo_ball (Schwarz lemma) applied to $f/(2M-f)$, then shifts by $f(0)$.

statement: Let $G$ be a complex semisimple group with [Borel subgroup](c:borel-subgroup) $B$ and Weyl group $W$, and $L_\lambda$ the [line bundle](c:line-bundle) of an integral weight $\lambda$ on the [flag variety](c:flag-variety) $G/B$, normalized so that dominant $\lambda$ have sections. If $\lambda+\rho$ is singular (fixed by a nontrivial element of $W$), all $H^i(G/B, L_\lambda)$ vanish. Otherwise $\mu = w(\lambda+\rho)-\rho$ is dominant for a unique $w \in W$, and $H^i$ vanishes unless $i = \ell(w)$, where it is irreducible of [highest weight](c:highest-weight) $\mu$.

hypotheses.text: $G$ is a complex semisimple algebraic group, $B$ a [Borel subgroup](c:borel-subgroup), and $G/B$ the [flag variety](c:flag-variety).
$\lambda$ is an integral weight and $L_\lambda$ is the [line bundle](c:line-bundle) on $G/B$ attached to it.

conclusion: The [sheaf cohomology](c:sheaf-cohomology) $H^i(G/B, L_\lambda)$ is $0$ for all $i$ if $\lambda+\rho$ is singular. Otherwise it is $0$ for $i \ne \ell(w)$, and for $i = \ell(w)$ it is the irreducible $G$-module of highest weight $w(\lambda+\rho) - \rho$.

proofs.name: Rank one reduction and descent
proofs.slogan: Reduce to the projective line along each simple reflection, then walk $\lambda + \rho$ into the dominant chamber and read the dominant case.
proofs.scope: An outline of Demazure's proof; the Leray spectral sequence and Borel-Weil in steps 2 and 4 rest on the cited work. Weights are written in the convention where dominant weights have sections.

roles.why: The minimal parabolics $P_\alpha \supseteq B$ give $\mathbb{P}^1$-fibrations of $G/B$, and semisimplicity gives the Weyl group action.
The integer $\langle \lambda, \alpha^\vee \rangle$ decides which cohomology of $L_\lambda$ the fibre $\mathbb{P}^1$ carries.

steps.slogan: Compute the cohomology of every line bundle $\mathcal{O}(n)$ on the projective line $\mathbb{P}^1$.
steps.detail: For $n \ge 0$, $H^0(\mathbb{P}^1, \mathcal{O}(n))$ is the irreducible $SL_2$-module of dimension $n+1$ and $H^1 = 0$. For $n \le -2$, Serre duality gives $H^1$ of dimension $-n-1$ and $H^0 = 0$. For $n = -1$ all cohomology vanishes.

steps.slogan: Move $\lambda$ by a simple reflection through the $\mathbb{P}^1$-fibration $G/B \to G/P_\alpha$ and shift the degree by one.
steps.detail: Let $n = \langle \lambda, \alpha^\vee \rangle$ and $\lambda' = s_\alpha(\lambda+\rho) - \rho$. By step 1 and the Leray spectral sequence, all cohomology of $L_\lambda$ vanishes if $n = -1$. If $n \ge 0$, then $H^i(L_\lambda) \cong H^{i+1}(L_{\lambda'})$. If $n \le -2$, the same rule read backwards gives $H^i(L_\lambda) \cong H^{i-1}(L_{\lambda'})$.

steps.slogan: Walk $\lambda + \rho$ toward the dominant chamber, one simple reflection at a time.
steps.detail: If $\lambda+\rho$ is not strictly dominant, some simple $\alpha$ has $n \le -1$. Either $n = -1$ and everything vanishes, or step 2 moves $\lambda$ one reflection closer and lowers the degree by one. A singular $\lambda+\rho$ always reaches a wall, so everything vanishes. A regular one reaches $\mu$ after $\ell(w)$ steps, with $H^i(L_\lambda) \cong H^{i-\ell(w)}(L_\mu)$.

steps.slogan: Compute the cohomology of $L_\mu$ for dominant $\mu$ by descending to the antidominant end.
steps.detail: Applying step 2 along a reduced word of the longest element $w_0$ gives $H^i(L_\mu) \cong H^{i+N}(L_{w_0 \cdot \mu})$ with $N = \dim G/B$. Cohomology vanishes above degree $N$, so $H^i(L_\mu) = 0$ for $i > 0$. The Borel-Weil theorem identifies $H^0(L_\mu)$ with the irreducible module of highest weight $\mu$.

steps.slogan: Combine the singular, regular and dominant cases into the theorem.
steps.detail: If $\lambda + \rho$ is singular, step 3 gives vanishing in all degrees. Otherwise $H^i(L_\lambda) \cong H^{i-\ell(w)}(L_\mu)$ by step 3, and step 4 says that this is zero unless $i = \ell(w)$, where it is irreducible of highest weight $\mu$.

concepts.c:borel-subgroup: Its minimal parabolic overgroups give the $\mathbb{P}^1$-fibrations of $G/B$.
concepts.c:line-bundle: The theorem computes the cohomology of line bundles $L_\lambda$.
concepts.c:flag-variety: The space $G/B$ fibres over $G/P_\alpha$ with fibre $\mathbb{P}^1$.
concepts.c:highest-weight: Highest weights label the irreducible modules that appear.
concepts.c:sheaf-cohomology: The Leray spectral sequence computes the cohomology groups $H^i$.

source.ref: M. Demazure, A very simple proof of Bott's theorem, Inventiones Mathematicae 33 (1976), 271-272
source.note: The theorem is due to R. Bott, Homogeneous vector bundles, Annals of Mathematics 66 (1957), 203-248 (doi 10.2307/1969996); Demazure's proof is the rank one reduction outlined here.

statement: Let $\mathcal{S}$ be a nonempty family of nonempty [compact](c:compact-space) [closed](c:closed-set) subsets of a topological space $X$ such that any two members contain a common member. Then $\bigcap \mathcal{S}$ is nonempty. For example, every decreasing sequence $K_0 \supseteq K_1 \supseteq \cdots$ of such sets has nonempty intersection.

hypotheses.text: $\mathcal{S}$ is a nonempty family of nonempty subsets of $X$, and any two members contain a common member.
Every member of $\mathcal{S}$ is [compact](c:compact-space).
Every member of $\mathcal{S}$ is [closed](c:closed-set) in $X$.

proofs.name: Finite subcover of one member
proofs.slogan: If the intersection were empty, the complements of the members would cover one compact member, and a finite subcover would give an empty member.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for any topological space and any directed family. A decreasing sequence is a directed family.

roles.why: Nonemptiness gives a first member $K_0$, and the common-member property gives one member inside a finite list.
Compactness of $K_0$ turns the cover by complements into a finite subcover.
Closedness makes each complement $X \setminus K$ an open set.

steps.slogan: Fix a member $K_0$ and suppose that $\bigcap \mathcal{S}$ is empty.
steps.detail: Choose any $K_0 \in \mathcal{S}$. Since $\bigcap \mathcal{S} \subseteq K_0$, the intersection is nonempty exactly when $K_0 \cap \bigcap \mathcal{S}$ is. Suppose for contradiction that this set is empty.

steps.slogan: Cover $K_0$ by the open complements $X \setminus K$ of the members $K \in \mathcal{S}$.
steps.detail: Every point of $K_0$ lies outside some member, because $K_0 \cap \bigcap \mathcal{S} = \emptyset$. So the sets $X \setminus K$ cover $K_0$, and each is open because $K$ is closed.

steps.slogan: Select a finite subcover of the compact set $K_0$.
steps.detail: By compactness, $K_0 \subseteq (X \setminus K_1) \cup \dots \cup (X \setminus K_r)$ for finitely many $K_j \in \mathcal{S}$. Equivalently $K_0 \cap K_1 \cap \dots \cap K_r = \emptyset$, so the family violates the [finite intersection property](c:finite-intersection-property).

steps.slogan: Find one member inside all of $K_0, \dots, K_r$ and reach a contradiction.
steps.detail: By induction on $r$, the common-member property gives $K \in \mathcal{S}$ with $K \subseteq K_0 \cap \dots \cap K_r = \emptyset$. This contradicts $K \ne \emptyset$, so $\bigcap \mathcal{S}$ is nonempty.

concepts.c:compact-space: Compactness of one member gives the finite subcover.
concepts.c:closed-set: Closed members have open complements, which form the cover.
concepts.c:finite-intersection-property: The finite subcover is a finite subfamily with empty intersection.

statement: Let a [linear elastic](c:linear-elasticity) body, held against rigid motion, carry forces $Q_1, \dots, Q_n$ applied slowly at fixed points. Let $\delta_i$ be the displacement of the point of $Q_i$ along $Q_i$, and write the [strain energy](c:strain-energy) $U$ as a function of $Q_1, \dots, Q_n$. Then $\delta_i = \partial U / \partial Q_i$ for every $i$.

hypotheses.text: The body is [linear elastic](c:linear-elasticity) and held against rigid motion, so each $\delta_i$ is a linear function $\sum_j c_{ij} Q_j$ of the forces.
The forces grow slowly from zero to their final values and no energy is lost, so the [strain energy](c:strain-energy) equals the work of the forces.

proofs.name: Quadratic energy in the forces
proofs.slogan: Write the strain energy as a quadratic form in the forces with a symmetric flexibility matrix, then differentiate.
proofs.scope: Castigliano's second theorem for point forces on a linear elastic body. The first theorem, $F_i = \partial U/\partial \delta_i$, is the dual statement and is not proved here.

roles.why: Linearity gives the flexibility matrix, and its symmetry follows from reciprocity.
Slow loading without losses makes the stored energy equal to the work integral.

steps.slogan: Equate the [strain energy](c:strain-energy) with the work of the slowly applied forces.
steps.detail: Load the body with $tQ_i$ for $t$ from $0$ to $1$. By linearity the displacements are $t\delta_i$, so the work is $\int_0^1 \sum_i Q_i \delta_i\, t\,dt = \tfrac12 \sum_i Q_i \delta_i$. With no losses, $U = \tfrac12 \sum_i Q_i \delta_i$ (Clapeyron's theorem).

steps.slogan: Write the displacements through a symmetric flexibility matrix.
steps.detail: Linearity gives $\delta_i = \sum_j c_{ij} Q_j$, where $c_{ij}$ is the displacement at point $i$ under a unit force at point $j$. Betti's reciprocal theorem gives $c_{ij} = c_{ji}$.

steps.slogan: Substitute the flexibility matrix to write $U$ as a [quadratic form](c:quadratic-form) in the forces.
steps.detail: Putting $\delta_i = \sum_j c_{ij} Q_j$ into $U = \tfrac12 \sum_i Q_i \delta_i$ gives $U = \tfrac12 \sum_{i,j} c_{ij} Q_i Q_j$. The coefficients $c_{ij}$ form a [symmetric matrix](c:symmetric-matrix).

steps.slogan: Take the [partial derivative](c:partial-derivative) of $U$ with respect to $Q_k$.
steps.detail: The product rule gives $\partial U/\partial Q_k = \tfrac12 \sum_j (c_{kj} + c_{jk}) Q_j$. By symmetry this equals $\sum_j c_{kj} Q_j = \delta_k$.

concepts.c:linear-elasticity: Linearity of displacements in forces gives the flexibility matrix.
concepts.c:strain-energy: The strain energy is the function whose derivative gives the displacement.
concepts.c:quadratic-form: Linear elasticity makes the energy a quadratic form in the forces.
concepts.c:symmetric-matrix: Symmetry of the flexibility matrix makes the derivative equal $\delta_k$.
concepts.c:partial-derivative: The displacement is the partial derivative of the energy in its force.

source.note: The standard derivation from Clapeyron's theorem and Betti's reciprocal theorem.

new_concepts.name: strain energy
new_concepts.reminder: Strain energy is the energy that an elastic body stores when loads deform it.
new_concepts.definition: The strain energy of a deformed elastic body is the work that the loads do when they deform the body slowly from rest. The body releases this energy when the loads are removed.

new_concepts.name: linear elasticity
new_concepts.reminder: A linear elastic body responds to loads with displacements that are proportional to the loads.
new_concepts.definition: A body is linear elastic when it returns to its rest shape after unloading and its stresses are linear functions of its strains. Then displacements at fixed points are linear functions of the applied forces.

statement: Let $(a_k)$ and $(b_l)$ be sequences in $\mathbb{R}$, $\mathbb{C}$ or another regular Hausdorff topological semiring. If $(a_k)$, $(b_l)$ and the double family $(a_k b_l)_{(k,l) \in \mathbb{N}^2}$ are summable, then $\big(\sum_k a_k\big)\big(\sum_l b_l\big) = \sum_{n} \sum_{k+l=n} a_k b_l$. In $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ the double family is summable when both series have [absolute convergence](c:absolute-convergence).

hypotheses.text: The families $(a_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ and $(b_l)_{l \in \mathbb{N}}$ are summable.
The double family $(a_k b_l)_{(k,l) \in \mathbb{N}^2}$ is summable, as holds in $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ under [absolute convergence](c:absolute-convergence) of both series.

conclusion: The series $\sum_n \sum_{k+l=n} a_k b_l$ converges and equals $\big(\sum_k a_k\big)\big(\sum_l b_l\big)$.

formal.difference: Mathlib allows any index monoid with finite antidiagonals, such as $\mathbb{N}$, and any regular Hausdorff topological semiring. The statement here is the case of $\mathbb{N}$-indexed families.

proofs.name: Regroup the double sum by antidiagonals
proofs.slogan: Multiply the sums termwise into a sum over all pairs, then group the pairs into the finite antidiagonals $k + l = n$.
proofs.scope: The whole formula for summable families. In $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ with absolute convergence, the hypothesis on the double family holds.

roles.why: Summability of $(b_l)$ makes each row summable, and multiplication by $a_k$ is continuous.
Summability of the double family lets one sum it in any grouping.

steps.slogan: Multiply the two sums termwise to get the sum over all pairs $(k, l)$.
steps.detail: For fixed $k$, continuity of multiplication gives $a_k \sum_l b_l = \sum_l a_k b_l$, and each row is summable because $(b_l)$ is. Summing over $k$ and grouping the summable double family by rows gives $\big(\sum_k a_k\big)\big(\sum_l b_l\big) = \sum_{(k,l)} a_k b_l$.

steps.slogan: Partition $\mathbb{N}^2$ into the finite antidiagonals $D_n = \{(k, l) : k + l = n\}$.
steps.detail: Every pair $(k, l)$ lies in exactly one $D_n$, namely $n = k + l$, and $D_n$ has $n + 1$ elements. So $\mathbb{N}^2$ is in bijection with the disjoint union of the $D_n$.

steps.slogan: Sum the summable double family by its antidiagonal groups.
steps.detail: A summable family can be summed group by group, so $\sum_{(k,l)} a_k b_l = \sum_n \sum_{(k,l) \in D_n} a_k b_l$, and the outer series converges. The inner sums are finite. For coefficients of two [power series](c:power-series), this is the coefficient of the product series.

concepts.c:absolute-convergence: It is the usual way to know that the double family is summable.
concepts.c:power-series: The formula gives the coefficients of a product of power series.

statement: Let $T \colon X \to Y$ be a bounded linear operator between [Banach spaces](c:banach-space), with [adjoint](c:adjoint-operator) $T' \colon Y^* \to X^*$. These conditions are equivalent: (a) $\operatorname{ran} T$ is closed; (b) $\operatorname{ran} T'$ is closed; (c) $\operatorname{ran} T = {}^{\perp}(\ker T')$; (d) $\operatorname{ran} T' = (\ker T)^{\perp}$. Here $\perp$ denotes the [annihilator](c:annihilator).

hypotheses.text: The spaces $X$ and $Y$ are [Banach spaces](c:banach-space).
The operator $T \colon X \to Y$ is linear and bounded, so its [adjoint](c:adjoint-operator) $T'$ is defined.

proofs.name: Open mapping and Hahn-Banach
proofs.slogan: Duality with Hahn-Banach gives (a) and (c); the open mapping theorem gives (d); a bound on $T'$ from below plus successive approximation returns (a) from (b).
proofs.scope: Bounded operators between Banach spaces. The closed densely defined case (Kato, Perturbation Theory for Linear Operators, chapter IV) needs the graph norm and is not proved here.

roles.why: Completeness of $X$ and of $Z$ drives the open mapping theorem and the successive approximation.
Boundedness defines $T'$ and gives $\ker T' = (\operatorname{ran} T)^\perp$.

steps.slogan: Identify $\ker T'$ with the [annihilator](c:annihilator) of $\operatorname{ran} T$ and apply Hahn-Banach.
steps.detail: A functional $\phi$ lies in $\ker T'$ exactly when $\phi(Tx) = 0$ for all $x$, so $\ker T' = (\operatorname{ran} T)^\perp$. By Hahn-Banach, ${}^\perp((\operatorname{ran} T)^\perp) = \overline{\operatorname{ran} T}$. So ${}^\perp(\ker T') = \overline{\operatorname{ran} T}$, which gives (a) $\Leftrightarrow$ (c).

steps.slogan: Show that a closed range gives $\operatorname{ran} T' = (\ker T)^\perp$, which is closed.
steps.detail: Always $\operatorname{ran} T' \subseteq (\ker T)^\perp$. If $\operatorname{ran} T$ is closed, the open mapping theorem makes $X/\ker T \to \operatorname{ran} T$ an isomorphism. A functional $x^* \in (\ker T)^\perp$ then defines a functional on $\operatorname{ran} T$, and Hahn-Banach extends it to $y^*$ with $T'y^* = x^*$. This gives (a) $\Rightarrow$ (d) $\Rightarrow$ (b).

steps.slogan: Assume (b), pass to dense range, and bound $T'$ from below.
steps.detail: Let $Z = \overline{\operatorname{ran} T}$ and $T_0 \colon X \to Z$. Then $T_0'$ is injective, and its range equals $\operatorname{ran} T'$, which is closed. The open mapping theorem applied to $T_0' \colon Z^* \to \operatorname{ran} T_0'$ gives $c > 0$ with $\|T_0'\phi\| \ge c\|\phi\|$.

steps.slogan: Separate to show that the image of the unit ball is dense in the $c$-ball of $Z$.
steps.detail: Let $K = \overline{T(B_X)}$, which is closed, convex and symmetric. If $z_0 \in Z$ with $\|z_0\| < c$ is not in $K$, Hahn-Banach gives $\phi \in Z^*$ with $\phi(z_0) > \sup_K \phi = \|T_0'\phi\| \ge c\|\phi\|$. But $\phi(z_0) \le \|z_0\|\|\phi\| < c\|\phi\|$, a contradiction. So $cB_Z \subseteq K$.

steps.slogan: Pass from a dense image to surjectivity by successive approximation in $X$.
steps.detail: Let $\|z\| < c$. Choose $x_1 \in B_X$ with $\|z - Tx_1\| < c/2$, then $x_2$ with $\|x_2\| \le 1/2$ and $\|z - Tx_1 - Tx_2\| < c/4$, and so on. Then $\sum x_k$ converges because $X$ is complete, and $T(\sum x_k) = z$. So $T_0$ is onto and $\operatorname{ran} T = Z$ is closed.

steps.slogan: Join the implications into one cycle of equivalences.
steps.detail: Step 1 gives (a) $\Leftrightarrow$ (c). Step 2 gives (a) $\Rightarrow$ (d) $\Rightarrow$ (b), and steps 3 to 5 give (b) $\Rightarrow$ (a). So the four conditions are equivalent.

concepts.c:banach-space: Completeness drives the open mapping theorem and the series in step 5.
concepts.c:adjoint-operator: The adjoint $T'$ carries the dual statements (b) and (d).
concepts.c:annihilator: Annihilators express $\ker T'$ and the closure of $\operatorname{ran} T$.

source.note: The textbook proof, as in Rudin, Functional Analysis, chapter 4 (closed range theorem).

statement: Let $E$ be a [finite-dimensional](c:finite-dimensional-vector-space) real normed space, $C \subseteq E$ an open [convex set](c:convex-set), and $f \colon C \to \mathbb{R}$ a [convex function](c:convex-function). Then $f$ is continuous on $C$.

hypotheses.text: The space $E$ is a real normed space of finite dimension.
The set $C \subseteq E$ is open and [convex](c:convex-set).
The function $f \colon C \to \mathbb{R}$ is [convex](c:convex-function).

conclusion: The function $f$ is continuous at every point of $C$.

proofs.name: Local Lipschitz bound
proofs.slogan: Bound a convex function above on a simplex, then bound its absolute value on a ball, and read a Lipschitz constant from extended chords.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; for $C = \emptyset$ there is nothing to prove. Finite dimension is used only in step 1, and infinite-dimensional spaces have discontinuous linear, hence convex, functionals.

roles.why: Finite dimension gives a simplex with finitely many vertices around each point.
Openness puts a small simplex and the extended chord points inside $C$.
Convexity bounds values inside a segment or simplex by the endpoint values.

steps.slogan: Place a [simplex](c:simplex) with vertices in $C$ around a point $x_0 \in C$.
steps.detail: Since $E$ is finite dimensional, there is an affine basis $b_0, \dots, b_d$ whose convex hull contains a neighbourhood of $x_0$. Since $C$ is open and convex, we may take the basis so close to $x_0$ that the hull lies in $C$.

steps.slogan: Bound $f$ above near $x_0$ by its largest value at the vertices.
steps.detail: A point $y$ of the hull is $y = \sum t_i b_i$ with $t_i \ge 0$ and $\sum t_i = 1$. Convexity gives $f(y) \le \sum t_i f(b_i) \le \max_i f(b_i)$.

steps.slogan: Bound $|f|$ on a ball around every point of $C$.
steps.detail: For $x \in C$ pick $y \in C$ with $x$ strictly between $y$ and $x_0$. Points $z$ near $x$ lie on segments from $y$ to points near $x_0$, so $f(z) \le \max(M_0, f(y))$. Then $f(z) \ge 2f(x) - f(2x - z)$ bounds $f$ below near $x$.

steps.slogan: Turn the bound $|f| \le M$ on $B(x, r)$ into a [Lipschitz](c:lipschitz-continuous-function) estimate by extending chords.
steps.detail: For $p \ne q$ in $B(x, r - \varepsilon)$ let $d = \|p - q\|$ and $z = p + \varepsilon (p - q)/d \in B(x, r)$. The point $p$ lies on the segment from $q$ to $z$, so convexity gives $\varepsilon (f(p) - f(q)) \le d\,(f(z) - f(p)) \le 2Md$. Swapping $p$ and $q$ gives $|f(p) - f(q)| \le (2M/\varepsilon)\,d$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that a function with a Lipschitz bound near every point is continuous.
steps.detail: By step 4, each point of $C$ has a ball on which $f$ is Lipschitz. For $\varepsilon' > 0$, take $\delta = \varepsilon' / K$ in that ball, where $K$ is the Lipschitz constant. So $f$ is continuous at the point.

concepts.c:finite-dimensional-vector-space: It supplies the simplex around each point.
concepts.c:convex-set: Convexity of $C$ keeps simplices and segments inside $C$.
concepts.c:convex-function: Convexity bounds $f$ on simplices, segments and extended chords.
concepts.c:simplex: The simplex has finitely many vertices that bound $f$ above.
concepts.c:lipschitz-continuous-function: A Lipschitz bound near each point gives continuity.

statement: Let $a \ne 0$, $p = \frac{3ac - b^2}{3a^2}$ and $q = \frac{2b^3 - 9abc + 27a^2 d}{27a^3}$. Let $s^2 = \frac{q^2}{4} + \frac{p^3}{27}$ and let $u$ be a [cube root](c:cube-root) of $-\frac{q}{2} + s$, with $u \ne 0$ unless $p = q = 0$. With $\omega$ a primitive cube [root of unity](c:root-of-unity), the roots of $ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d$ over $\mathbb{C}$ are $\omega^k u - \frac{p}{3\omega^k u} - \frac{b}{3a}$ for $k = 0, 1, 2$.

hypotheses.text: The coefficients $a, b, c, d$ are [complex numbers](c:complex-number) and $a \ne 0$.
The number $u$ is a [cube root](c:cube-root) of $-q/2 + s$, where $s^2 = q^2/4 + p^3/27$ and $u \ne 0$ unless $p = q = 0$.

conclusion: Counted with multiplicity, the roots are $x_k = \omega^k u - p/(3\omega^k u) - b/(3a)$ for $k = 0, 1, 2$. If $p = q = 0$, the only root is $-b/(3a)$, with multiplicity $3$.

proofs.name: Cardano's substitution
proofs.slogan: Remove the square term, split the unknown as $u + v$ with $3uv = -p$, solve a quadratic for $u^3$, and read all roots from the cube roots of unity.
proofs.scope: The case $p = q = 0$ is separate: then $t^3 = 0$ and $x = -b/(3a)$ is a triple root. Otherwise a suitable $s$ exists, because $-q/2 + s = 0$ forces $p = 0$, and then the other sign gives $u^3 = -q \ne 0$.

roles.why: The condition $a \ne 0$ allows division by $a$ and by $3a$ in the shift.
The choice of $s$ and $u$ gives $u^3$ and $v^3$ and a nonzero $u$ to divide by.

steps.slogan: Shift $x = t - b/(3a)$ to remove the square term.
steps.detail: Expanding $a(t - \frac{b}{3a})^3 + b(t - \frac{b}{3a})^2 + c(t - \frac{b}{3a}) + d$ and dividing by $a$ gives $t^3 + pt + q$ with $p$ and $q$ as stated.

steps.slogan: Write $t = u + v$ with $3uv = -p$ to turn the cubic into a sum of cubes.
steps.detail: Since $t^3 = u^3 + v^3 + 3uv(u + v) = u^3 + v^3 - pt$, we get $t^3 + pt + q = u^3 + v^3 + q$. So $t$ is a root as soon as $u^3 + v^3 = -q$ and $uv = -p/3$.

steps.slogan: Find $u^3$ and $v^3$ as the two roots of a quadratic.
steps.detail: The numbers $u^3, v^3$ have sum $-q$ and product $-p^3/27$, so they are the roots $-q/2 \pm s$ of $z^2 + qz - p^3/27$. Take $u^3 = -q/2 + s$ and $v = -p/(3u)$. Then $v^3 = -q/2 - s$, because $(-q/2 + s)(-q/2 - s) = q^2/4 - s^2 = -p^3/27$.

steps.slogan: Replace $u$ by $\omega^k u$ and $v$ by $\omega^{-k} v$ to get three roots.
steps.detail: The numbers $\omega^k u$ and $\omega^{-k} v$ have the same cubes and the same product $uv$ as $u$ and $v$. So by step 2, each $t_k = \omega^k u + \omega^{-k} v$ is a root of $t^3 + pt + q$.

steps.slogan: Check by Vieta's formulas that the $t_k$ are all the roots with multiplicity.
steps.detail: We have $\sum t_k = 0$, $\sum_{j<k} t_j t_k = -\tfrac12 \sum t_k^2 = -3uv = p$ and $t_0 t_1 t_2 = u^3 + v^3 = -q$. So $\prod (t - t_k) = t^3 + pt + q$. This holds even when roots coincide, that is, when the [discriminant](c:discriminant) $-108 s^2$ is zero.

steps.slogan: Shift back by $-b/(3a)$ to read the roots of the original cubic.
steps.detail: By step 1, the roots of $ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d$ are $x_k = t_k - b/(3a)$, with the same multiplicities. Substituting $v = -p/(3u)$ gives the stated formula.

concepts.c:cube-root: Cube roots of $-q/2 + s$ give $u$ and the other two choices.
concepts.c:root-of-unity: Cube roots of unity rotate $u$ and $v$ into the other two roots.
concepts.c:complex-number: Complex numbers contain the square and cube roots that the formula needs.
concepts.c:discriminant: A zero discriminant means repeated roots, which Vieta's formulas still count.

source.note: Cardano's method (Ars Magna, 1545), in its modern form with Vieta's formulas.

statement: For a connected [CW complex](c:cw-complex) $X$, the [homotopy groups](c:homotopy-group) of the infinite [symmetric product](c:symmetric-product) $SP(X) = \operatorname{colim}_n SP^n(X)$ are the reduced [homology](c:homology) groups: $\pi_n SP(X) \cong \tilde H_n(X; \mathbb{Z})$ for every $n \ge 1$.

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is a connected [CW complex](c:cw-complex) with a base point.

conclusion: For every $n \ge 1$ there is an isomorphism $\pi_n SP(X) \cong \tilde H_n(X; \mathbb{Z})$, natural in $X$.

proofs.name: Homotopy groups of SP form a homology theory
proofs.slogan: Show that $X \mapsto \pi_n SP(X)$ is a reduced homology theory on connected CW complexes with the coefficients of $\mathbb{Z}$, then use uniqueness of homology.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof; the quasifibration theorem in step 2 rests on the cited work. Connectedness makes $SP(X)$ a connected H-space with a base point.

roles.why: The CW structure gives homotopy invariance, the quotient $X/A$ for subcomplexes, and the uniqueness theorem for homology.

steps.slogan: Show that $SP$ is functorial and preserves homotopy equivalences of CW complexes.
steps.detail: A map $X \to Y$ induces $SP(X) \to SP(Y)$ on each $SP^n$, and a homotopy of maps induces a homotopy of the induced maps. So a homotopy equivalence of CW complexes induces one of their [symmetric products](c:symmetric-product).

steps.slogan: Show that $SP(X) \to SP(X/A)$ is a [quasifibration](c:quasifibration) with fibre $SP(A)$ for a CW pair.
steps.detail: For connected CW pairs $(X, A)$, the Dold-Thom criterion applied along the filtration by the subspaces $SP^n$ makes the projection $SP(X) \to SP(X/A)$ a quasifibration with fibre $SP(A)$. Its long exact sequence of [homotopy groups](c:homotopy-group) is $\cdots \to \pi_n SP(A) \to \pi_n SP(X) \to \pi_n SP(X/A) \to \pi_{n-1} SP(A) \to \cdots$.

steps.slogan: Check that $h_n(X) = \pi_n SP(X)$ satisfies the axioms of a reduced homology theory on connected CW complexes.
steps.detail: Homotopy invariance is step 1 and exactness is step 2. Excision holds because the sequence involves $X/A$. Wedge sums satisfy $SP(X \vee Y) \simeq SP(X) \times SP(Y)$, which gives additivity and the suspension isomorphism.

steps.slogan: Compute the coefficients from $SP(S^1) \simeq S^1$ and the suspension isomorphism.
steps.detail: The product of circle points shows $SP(S^1) \simeq S^1$, so $h_1(S^1) = \mathbb{Z}$ and $h_k(S^1) = 0$ for $k \ne 1$. By the suspension isomorphism, $h_k(S^n) = \mathbb{Z}$ for $k = n$ and $0$ otherwise, so $SP(S^n)$ is an [Eilenberg-Mac Lane space](c:eilenberg-maclane-space) $K(\mathbb{Z}, n)$.

steps.slogan: Conclude from the uniqueness of homology theories on CW complexes that $h_n \cong \tilde H_n(-;\mathbb{Z})$.
steps.detail: Two reduced homology theories on connected CW complexes with the same coefficients are naturally isomorphic, by induction over skeleta and the five lemma. So $\pi_n SP(X) \cong \tilde H_n(X; \mathbb{Z})$ for every connected CW complex $X$.

concepts.c:cw-complex: Uniqueness of homology holds on CW complexes, by induction over skeleta.
concepts.c:homotopy-group: The groups $\pi_n SP(X)$ are the values of the theory.
concepts.c:symmetric-product: The symmetric product is the functor whose homotopy groups the theorem computes.
concepts.c:homology: Homology is the theory to which $\pi_n SP$ is shown isomorphic.
concepts.c:quasifibration: A quasifibration gives the long exact sequence of the theory.
concepts.c:eilenberg-maclane-space: The coefficient computation shows that $SP(S^n)$ is a $K(\mathbb{Z}, n)$.

source.ref: A. Dold and R. Thom, Quasifaserungen und unendliche symmetrische Produkte, Annals of Mathematics 67 (1958), 239-281
source.note: Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, section 4.K, gives a textbook account of the same route through quasifibrations.
